In the present study, we mutated the negatively charged amino acids D91, D97, E110, and D114 as well as the neutral polar amino acid Y161 to code for alanine with a neutral hydrophobic side chain or lysine with a positively charged side chain and performed patch-clamp analysis as well as surface GlyR staining using transfected HEK293T cells. We found that substitutions D97A/K and Y161K resulted in a complete loss of receptor function in response to glycine or Cs+, whereas mutations at D91 and E110 retained detectable current responses, with E110A/K mainly affecting glycine-evoked currents. Y161A retained at least some Cs+-dependent GlyR responsiveness at concentrations above 5 mM, indicating that a positive charge (K) at position Y161 is detrimental to glycine-dependent GlyR activation. However, as no mutant was identified that responded to glycine while lacking Cs+-evoked activity, these findings suggest that Cs+-mediated GlyR activation involves the same structural framework required for glycine-induced channel opening.

title: Effect of music on short-term pain perception during peripheral intravenous cannulation.
abstract: There is no general consensus on which music genre is most effective for a specific condition. The impact of music on subjective pain perception during intravenous cannulation for a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan was investigated. 204 patients were assigned to one of four groups: listening to Mozart, favorite music, relaxation music, or no music (control). Pain was assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale at four time points. Favorite music significantly reduced pain perception both 30 s and 2 min after puncture while Mozart showed a trend towards reduced pain perception 2 min after puncture. When including only patients with baseline pain (n = 71), a significant pain reduction was also observed in the Mozart group 2 min, with borderline significance 30 s after puncture, whereas the favorite music group not only intensified reduced pain perception 30 s and 2 min but also caused significant pain reduction immediately after puncture. No effect on pain was found for the relaxation music and control groups. Music may be effective for pain relief in unpleasant settings involving short painful interventions. Favorite music should be considered first, whereby patients with baseline pain could also benefit from listening to Mozart, indicating a potential "Mozart effect" in this subgroup. These exploratory results need to be validated in future studies including a higher number of patients.

title: Multiple sclerosis relapse following gamma knife radiosurgery for meningioma in a patient treated with natalizumab: case report.
abstract: We describe a case of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) stable on natalizumab who developed widespread gadolinium-enhancing lesions and clinical relapse seven and eight months after gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for left cerebellar convexity meningioma. We explore how increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability post-GKRS could potentially interfere with the lymphocyte anti-trafficking effect of natalizumab and result in new central nervous system (CNS) inflammation distant from the radiation site. Comprehensive analysis of the patient's chart, brain and spine imaging, serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiles was conducted. We compiled a graphical representation of treatment changes, radiologic findings, and GKRS initiation within one timeframe. We conducted a structured literature review to support the discussion of this case and hypothesize possible pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to clinical and radiological findings. Seven months after GKRS, follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, and repeat imaging one month later revealed new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, correlating with the patient's clinical relapse. Alternative causes of disease progression, including radiation-induced demyelination, radionecrosis, opportunistic infections, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and development of anti-natalizumab antibodies, were explored and considered less likely. The patient was switched to ofatumumab with subsequent clinical and radiological stability. Given extensive new inflammatory lesions far from the GKRS site, it seems unlikely that the sole mechanism was radiation-induced neurotoxicity. We hypothesize that late delayed radiation side effects caused by GKRS may have enabled peripheral lymphocytes to enter the CNS, counteracting the effects of natalizumab on blocking lymphocyte trafficking through the BBB and possibly contributing to MS relapse.

title: Immunometabolic synaptopathy: linking metabolic syndrome to epileptogenesis through trained immunity and parvalbumin interneuron vulnerability.
abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) and epilepsy are clinically associated, but how chronic peripheral metabolic stress might influence seizure susceptibility remains unclear. The potential links among CNS-interface dysfunction, glial responses, and inhibitory-circuit vulnerability require further clarification. We propose immunometabolic synaptopathy as a hypothesis-driven framework linking chronic metabolic dysfunction to impaired inhibitory-circuit resilience. MetS-associated metabolic and inflammatory signals may alter blood-brain barrier function, CNS-border immune signaling, and glial homeostasis. Evidence from peripheral myeloid training and CNS immune-memory models supports the plausibility of trained-immunity-like microglial priming, but its occurrence and persistence in MetS-associated epileptogenesis remain unestablished. We identify the parvalbumin-positive interneuron-perineuronal net (PV-PNN) unit as a candidate convergence point because of its energetic demands and dependence on ionic and extracellular-matrix homeostasis. Altered metabolic and trophic support, oxidative stress, impaired K+ and glutamate handling, and PNN remodeling may jointly compromise PV-mediated inhibition. Whether these processes preferentially affect PV-PNN units or precede spontaneous seizures requires direct testing. Five candidate nodes-NLRP3, mTOR, HIF-1α, MMP-9, and Kir4.1-provide opportunities for mechanistic testing. Their therapeutic relevance to MetS-associated epilepsy remains uncertain, and available compounds differ in selectivity, CNS exposure, and safety. The framework motivates experimental evaluation of intervention timing and target dependence rather than specific clinical treatment recommendations. Immunometabolic synaptopathy integrates cross-context evidence into a testable hypothesis of metabolically associated seizure susceptibility. The complete pathway to spontaneous epilepsy has not been demonstrated end-to-end and requires longitudinal, cell- and pathway-specific validation.

title: Macroscopic cerebral energy efficiency corresponds to neuron reorganization in awake and anesthetized mice.
abstract: Non-invasive imaging of brain function and energy supply is crucial for diagnosing and treating brain disorders. Conventional imaging struggles to capture altered relationships between energy supply and demand caused by brain diseases. A novel method, thus far only tested non-invasively in human subjects, is to calculate relative power (rPWR) and relative cost (rCST) to assess cerebral energy efficiency. However, whether rPWR/rCST tracks individual changes and relate to neural activity remains unproven. Our study examines awake and anesthetized male mice and compares rPWR/rCST with invasive two-photon microscopy. We found that rPWR/rCST distributions were similar between awake mice and humans, but changed in anesthetized mice, indicating a shift in the brain's economic balance. Furthermore, changes in rPWR/rCST were linked to the reorganization of microscopic neural networks, observed with two-photon microscopy. Our work highlights the potential of rPWR/rCST for medical applications, and that neural network reorganization is linked to the brain's economic balance.

title: Food for thought: food availability alters crayfish perception of fear and safety in risky habitats.
abstract: Recent evidence shows that prey behavior is mediated by information regarding predators, refuges, and possibly food. However, the ways in which these 3 factors influence prey behavior in tandem with one another is still largely unexplored. We exposed rusty crayfish (Faxonius rusticus) to largemouth bass (Micropterus nigricans) odors and quantified sheltering and foraging behaviors. We presented crayfish with shelters of varying quality in 2 spatial arrangements and changed the location of a food source, Chara spp., to be near each shelter in different treatments. In this way, we created both a gradient of fear and of safety independently from one another while attempting to alter the perception of these gradients with changes to food location. We found that predator odor, refuge spatial arrangement, and food location were all important for crayfish behaviors. First, we found that time sheltering and time near shelters were both significantly impacted by interactions of shelter quality and arrangement. Crayfish only spent more time in and near upstream high-quality shelters when Chara spp. was also upstream. Next, we found that the average gape ratio of bass used in trials significantly altered the total amount of Chara spp. consumed, time spent foraging, and crayfish movement. The results of this study show the importance of information related to risk, safety, and food in altering prey behaviors, and these factors are used in combination. Specifically, the presence of a food source and the proximity of a food source to a shelter may affect where and when a prey organism shelters.

title: The psychological configuration of suicidal ideation in depressive disorder: an integrative and predictive approach.
abstract: Suicidal ideation in depression is increasingly understood as a multidetermined phenomenon shaped by emotional distress, emotion regulation deficits, maladaptive coping, and contextual vulnerability. The present study examined the psychological correlates and predictors of suicidal ideation and tested the mediating roles of emotion regulation difficulties and quality of life in adults with depressive disorder. A cross-sectional study was conducted on 172 adults with depressive disorder. Participants completed standardized measures of suicidal ideation and suicidal behavior (C-SSRS), depressive severity (MADRS), emotional distress (DASS-21R), emotion regulation difficulties (DERS-SF), coping strategies (Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire [CERQ] and Strategic Approach to Coping Scale [SACS]), and quality of life (QOLI). Spearman correlations, hierarchical regression analyses, and mediation models with bootstrapping (5,000 samples) were performed. Suicidal ideation was positively associated with depressive severity, anxiety, stress, several dimensions of emotion regulation difficulties, and maladaptive coping strategies, and negatively associated with quality of life. Hierarchical regression analyses identified depressive severity and quality of life as the most robust contributors in the first model, while maladaptive behavioral and cognitive coping strategies contributed additional explanatory value in the second model. Mediation analyses indicated that emotion regulation difficulties significantly mediated the association between depressive severity and suicidal ideation, and that a significant serial indirect effect also operated through reduced quality of life. In both models, the direct effect of depressive severity remained significant, indicating partial mediation. Suicidal ideation in depressive disorder is associated with a broader psychological configuration involving emotional distress, emotion regulation difficulties, maladaptive coping, and diminished quality of life. These findings support an integrative, multivariable approach to understanding suicidal ideation in depression and highlight clinically relevant psychological factors that may inform assessment and intervention.

title: Cannabidiol preserves astrocyte viability and attenuates injury-induced glial stress responses across zebra finch song control nuclei.
abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation following traumatic brain injury (TBI) increases the risk of affective disorders and early-onset dementias. Existing anti-inflammatory therapies are limited by systemic side effects with chronic use and by poor brain penetration of newer biologics. Cannabidiol (CBD), a non-euphorigenic phytocannabinoid with a favorable safety profile and multi-target neuroprotective actions, is a promising alternative. Using a songbird microlesion model of learned vocal recovery after targeted damage to the premotor nucleus HVC, we previously showed that systemic CBD (10 mg/kg/day) reduces vocal disruption, inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, and synaptic loss. Here we tested the hypothesis that these benefits involve astrocytes. CBD (10 mg/kg/day IM for 7 days) preserved astrocyte viability, attenuated injury-induced lysosomal stress, suppressed reactivity markers (C3, S100A10, aromatase), and upregulated key metabolic and antioxidant transcripts (glutamine synthetase and GCLM) across the interconnected song-control nuclei HVC, RA, and Area X. These changes were accompanied by reduced neuronal apoptosis in lesioned HVC. The results identify astrocyte-associated responses as a candidate cellular substrate of CBD's circuit-wide protective effects and support its translational potential to mitigate secondary injury and communication deficits after TBI.

title: Understanding ChatGPT adoption among medical students: an integrated theoretical model of psychological barriers and individual factors.
abstract: The growing adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly ChatGPT, has created new opportunities for medical education by supporting learning, problem-solving, and knowledge acquisition. However, evidence regarding the psychological and individual factors influencing ChatGPT adoption among medical students remains limited. This study develops and tests an integrated theoretical model that combines Privacy Theory, Technostress Theory, Affect Theory, Diffusion of Innovation Theory, and the Theory of Planned Behavior to explain ChatGPT adoption. A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among undergraduate medical students at King Faisal University, Saudi Arabia using a structured, self-administered questionnaire. The proposed model examined the effects of privacy concern, technophobia, guilt feelings, and innovativeness on behavioral intention and ChatGPT usage behavior, with behavioral intention serving as the mediating variable. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings showed that innovativeness had a significant positive relationship with behavioral intention (β = 0.579, p < 0.001), while behavioral intention had a strong positive relationship with ChatGPT usage behavior (β = 0.777, p < 0.001). In addition, behavioral intention significantly mediated the relationship between innovativeness and ChatGPT usage behavior (β = 0.450, p < 0.001). In contrast, privacy concern, technophobia, and guilt feelings were not significantly related to behavioral intention, and their indirect relationships with ChatGPT usage behavior were also not significant. Within the proposed model, personal innovativeness was the only antecedent significantly associated with behavioral intention, whereas the psychological barriers were not statistically significant. By integrating five complementary theoretical perspectives into a single framework, this study extends current understanding of generative AI adoption in medical education and highlights behavioral intention as the key mechanism linking individual characteristics to actual use. The findings provide theoretical insights and practical guidance for promoting the responsible and effective integration of ChatGPT into medical education through initiatives that foster innovativeness and AI literacy.

title: γ-Radiation induces long-term dose-related proteomic and phosphorylated-tau species changes in non-human primate hippocampus.
abstract: Long-term neurological consequences of acute total-body γ-radiation are poorly understood. Here we investigated the persistency of molecular changes in non-human primates (NHPs) 5+ years after single exposure to ~4 Gy or ~8 Gy total body irradiation dose. MS-based proteomic analyses were performed on samples of micro-dissected hippocampus from brains of irradiated/control NHPs. We used STRING and DAVID analyses to expand interpretation of proteomic data. Proteomic findings were further assessed using Western blot and digital-PCR. Proteomic analysis of the hippocampus revealed profound, dose-dependent molecular changes. ~4 Gy primarily impacted synaptic plasticity, while ~8 Gy affected catabolism, vascular development, and inflammation. Apelin receptor (APLNR) was the only protein consistently lowered at both radiation doses, suggesting it may be a key biomarker for radiation-induced brain injury. Significantly, while most proteins linked to neurodegeneration were unchanged, Tau (MAPT) protein levels increased at ~8 Gy, and some animals developed Tau-positive lesions resembling neurofibrillary tangles. Moreover, we found complex, dose-specific alterations in phosphorylated forms of other key proteins (alpha-synuclein, TDP-43). Overall, these findings show that different radiation doses induce distinct, persistent molecular changes in NHP hippocampus. This work highlights dysregulation of proteins usually associated with neurodegeneration (i.e., Tau and synaptic proteins) as a major long-term consequence of radiation, providing new insights into the molecular shift that accompany post-exposure high-dose radiation and likely a possible cause of post-exposure cognitive deficits.

title: Corneal Confocal Microscopy (CCM) in Patients With Central Neurodegenerative Disease.
abstract: Corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) is a rapid, non-invasive ophthalmic imaging technique that enables detailed visualization and quantification of small corneal nerve fibres. Although initially developed for the assessment of diabetic neuropathy, its application has broadened substantially, with increasing evidence supporting its value in a range of central neurodegenerative diseases. This narrative review synthesizes current findings on the use of CCM in dementia, multiple sclerosis, stroke, burning mouth syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, trigeminal neuralgia, migraine and Parkinson's disease. Across these conditions, CCM consistently identifies measurable alterations in corneal nerve fibre density, length, branching and morphology, as well as changes in corneal immune cell populations. These structural abnormalities frequently correlate with disease severity, functional decline and clinical progression. In some disorders, CCM demonstrates diagnostic performance comparable to or exceeding existing biomarkers, and offers distinct advantages as a non-invasive, repeatable and objective measure that can detect early or subclinical neurodegeneration. Corneal confocal microscopy also shows potential as a prognostic and monitoring tool, particularly in conditions with limited reliable biomarkers. It may help stratify risk, track therapeutic response, and provide surrogate endpoints for clinical trials. Despite these strengths, several limitations remain, including modest sample sizes in some studies, variability in image interpretation, and difficulties differentiating between neurodegenerative conditions with overlapping patterns of nerve loss. Emerging automated analysis methods and artificial intelligence-based algorithms may help address these challenges by improving accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. Overall, CCM represents a promising technique that bridges ophthalmology and neurology. A growing body of literature supports its utility across multiple neurodegenerative diseases, and further large-scale, longitudinal studies may help establish its role within routine clinical assessment and research.

title: Past wounds, present bonds, future mothers: item-level analysis of perinatal risk profiles.
abstract: Perinatal depression is shaped by interacting psycho-relational risk factors-childhood adversity, current relational functioning, perceived social support, and prenatal attachment. Variable-centered approaches focused on isolated predictors may obscure how these dimensions combine within individuals to generate distinct vulnerability configurations. To identify person-centered profiles of psychosocial functioning during pregnancy and to examine their association with depressive symptoms across the perinatal period. A sample of 774 pregnant women was recruited from full-term and high-risk pregnancy clinics at one of the largest birth centers in Southern Italy. A subsample of 200 women (25.8%) completed the postpartum follow-up at 6 months (T1). An item-level k-means cluster analysis (k = 3) was performed on 44 items from the CTQ-SF, DAS-7, MSSS, and MAAS. Cluster differences in EPDS scores were tested cross-sectionally with one-way ANOVA and a covariate-adjusted model (T0), and longitudinally with a repeated-measures ANOVA (T0-T1). A formal attrition analysis and domain-level sensitivity analyses were also conducted. Three profiles emerged: Low-Risk (53.7%), Moderately Adjusted (31.7%), and High-Adversity (14.6%). Between-cluster differences in depressive symptoms were significant at T0 (F(2, 771) = 62.52, p < 0.001, η 2 = 0.140), were essentially unchanged after adjustment for sociodemographic and obstetric covariates (F(2, 747) = 58.15, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.135), and persisted across the perinatal period (main effect of cluster: F(2, 197) = 22.74, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.188), with no significant Time effect (F(1, 197) = 0.38, p = 0.54) or Cluster × Time interaction (F(2, 197) = 1.40, p = 0.25). At T0, 11.1, 35.9, and 44.2% of the Low-Risk, Moderately Adjusted, and High-Adversity profiles, respectively, scored above the EPDS clinical cut-off (≥ 9; p < 0.001). Item-level cluster analysis reveals clinically significant heterogeneity in perinatal risk. Between-profile differences in depressive symptoms persisted across the perinatal period and may inform stratified, trauma-informed prevention strategies.

title: 3-[[4-(Benzylamino)quinazolin-2-yl] Amino] Benzenesulfonamide, a Quinazoline-Based PDE5 Inhibitor, Induces Vasorelaxation in Rat Mesenteric Arteries via Multiple Mechanisms.
abstract: We synthesised a series of N2,N4-diaminoquinazoline derivatives, among which 3-[[4-(benzylamino)quinazolin-2-yl]amino]benzenesulfonamide (compound 5) exhibited potent phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitory activity. Increasing evidence suggests that PDE5 inhibition is a promising therapeutic strategy for peripheral vascular disease. This study aimed to investigate vasorelaxant effects of 5 and its underlying mechanisms in rat mesenteric arteries. Compound 5 was synthesised and purified, and evaluated its vascular activity using organ bath assay. Molecular docking was performed to identify its potential molecular targets. Compound 5 (0.0001-30 μM) induced relaxation of phenylephrine (PE)-precontracted mesenteric arteries (EC50 = 0.76 ± 0.29 μM; Emax = 95.6% ± 1.1%). This effect was attenuated by endothelium removal (EC50 = 5.24 ± 0.98 μM) and by L-NAME (eNOS inhibitor). Compound 5 enhanced sodium nitroprusside-induced relaxation, supporting modulation of the NO-sGC-cGMP axis via PDE5 inhibition. Iberiotoxin (BKCa blocker) reduced relaxation, whereas 4-aminopyridine (KV blocker) and glibenclamide (KATP blocker) had no effect. Compound 5 inhibited vasoconstriction mediated by extracellular Ca2+ influx via receptor-operated Ca2+ channels (ROCCs) and α1-adrenergic receptor activation. Molecular docking provided qualitative support for PDE5A, BKCa channels and α1-adrenergic receptor as potential targets. In conclusion, 5 induces potent vasorelaxation in resistance arteries through eNOS/NO/cGMP signalling, BKCa channel activation and inhibition of ROCCs and α1-adrenergic receptors, supporting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for peripheral vascular disorders.

title: The bidirectional predictive association between methamphetamine use and depression.
abstract: Co-occurrence of methamphetamine dependence and depression is high, though the direction of this temporal relationship is unclear. We investigated the direction of the temporal relationship between methamphetamine use and depression. A longitudinal random-intercept cross-lagged panel model analysis was conducted using 12 contiguous weeks of data from a randomised controlled trial (ACTRN12618000366257). Melbourne, Geelong and Wollongong, Australia. 153 adult participants dependent on methamphetamine. Each week, days of methamphetamine use in the past week were assessed using the Timeline Followback, and clinically significant symptoms of depression were defined as a score of 4 or greater on the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale depression item. Relative to their average, if an individual increased their methamphetamine use in one week, their probability of experiencing clinically significant depressive symptoms increased the following week [estimate = 0.271, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.177-0.365, P < 0.001]. Additionally, if an individual's probability of experiencing clinically significant depressive symptoms increased in one week above their average, their subsequent week's methamphetamine use increased (estimate = 0.414, 95% CI = 0.291-0.537, P < 0.001). There appears to be evidence of a bidirectional relationship between days of methamphetamine use and clinically significant depressive symptoms within a weekly timeframe.

title: Should Coffee Consumers Not Have Their Habitual Morning Coffee Before Testing Their Cognitive Functions?
abstract: Caffeine could improve cognitive functions, but study protocols usually prohibit drinking coffee before cognitive testing. However, regular coffee consumers may experience withdrawal effects when they cannot drink their habitual coffee, which may impair cognitive performance. Therefore, we tested the effects of overnight coffee abstinence in regular coffee consumers: once allowing to drink their coffee and once not drinking coffee. The cognitive performance was compared with non-regular coffee consumers. Thirty regular coffee consumers (RCCs) and 25 non-regular consumers (N-RCCs) took part in this study. RCCs were tested after their habitual morning coffee (c-RCC) and after overnight abstinence (a-RCC); N-RCCs were tested once. A cognitive battery assessed reaction time (RT), processing speed (digit symbol substitution test), working memory, verbal learning/memory and executive function (Stroop). Sleep quality was included as a covariate. Compared to c-RCC, overnight coffee abstinence significantly slowed RTs but did not affect the performance in the other cognitive tasks. In the a-RCC condition, but not the c-RCC condition, the RTs were slower than those of the N-RCCs, while accuracy measures were comparable across groups. Sleep quality did not alter these findings. Overnight coffee abstinence selectively slowed RT, and no statistical support was found for effects on memory or executive function. This suggests that overnight coffee abstinence protocols may introduce withdrawal-related RT slowing as a confound in habitual consumers, whereas other cognitive domains may not be affected. Allowing habitual consumers to maintain normal coffee intake could reduce this bias, supporting tailored rather than uniform abstinence requirements based on the specific outcomes studied.

title: CochleaNet: deep learning-based image analysis for cochlear connectomics and gene therapy.
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
abstract: With the emergence of gene and optogenetic therapies targeting deafness, the comprehensive analysis of the molecular anatomy and physiology of the cochlea has become ever more important. Here, we introduce CochleaNet, a deep learning-based framework to analyze volumetric imaging data obtained by light-sheet microscopy of decalcified, cleared and fluorescently labeled cochleae. CochleaNet covers the workflow from reconstruction of the cochlea to segmentation of inner hair cells, spiral ganglion neurons and their afferent synapses, to the analysis of tonotopy and specific fluorescent expression patterns. We validated CochleaNet by comparison to manual image analysis, also demonstrating its superiority to prior segmentation methods. We then analyzed different spiral ganglion neuron types and validated different gene therapy products with CochleaNet. Trained on high isotropic resolution mouse data, CochleaNet was also applicable to the cochlea of the gerbil, another relevant animal model, and lower-resolution mouse and marmoset data from a commercially available microscope. We conclude that the combination of light-sheet microscopy and image analysis with CochleaNet paves the way for rapid and reliable quantification of cochlear molecular anatomy and preclinical gene therapy outcomes.

title: The uncinate fasciculus in frontotemporal dementia subtypes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of diffusion-tensor imaging studies.
abstract: BackgroundFrontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-onset neurodegeneration with selective frontal and temporal lobe degeneration. Despite well-characterized gray and white matter atrophy patterns across FTD subtypes, the extent of degeneration of the uncinate fasciculus (UF) tract has not been systematically quantified across FTD subtypes.ObjectiveTo compare uncinate fasciculus fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, radial diffusivity, and axial diffusivity between frontotemporal dementia subtypes and healthy controls.MethodsWe systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of diffusion tensor imaging studies published between 2011 and October 2025 according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines.ResultsWe systematically reviewed 11 studies and performed a meta-analysis of 540 participants across 10 studies. We found that all FTD subtypes demonstrated significant degeneration of the UF compared to controls. The greatest effect sizes were observed when comparing the left UF between the semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) and controls (FA: SMD = -2.5396, 95% CI: -3.7914, -1.2878, p < 0.0001; RD: SMD = 2.2414, 95% CI:1.7972, 2.6855, p < 0.0001; AD: SMD = 1.9831, 95% CI: 1.1434, 2.8227, p < 0.0001; MD: SMD = 2.5268, 95% CI: 1.9993, 3.0542, p < 0.0001), while the behavioral variant (bvFTD) showed the largest reduction in right UF fractional anisotropy. Within-group analyses revealed significant left-right asymmetry in svPPA and non-fluent aphasia (nfvPPA), with greater left UF involvement, while bvFTD and controls showed no hemispheric differences.ConclusionsWe highlight the UF as a promising tract for understanding disease mechanisms and developing imaging biomarkers in FTD.

title: A five-gene mitochondrial-lipid metabolism signature for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis identified by machine learning and validated in independent cohorts.
abstract: BackgroundMitochondrial dysfunction and lipid metabolism dysregulation represent early key events in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet integrated transcriptomic signatures combining these two biological processes for AD diagnosis remain poorly defined.ObjectiveThis study aimed to construct and validate a mitochondrial-lipid metabolism (MLM) gene-based diagnostic classifier for AD using machine-learning approaches and explore its underlying biological mechanisms.MethodsTwo public GEO datasets GSE5281 (training) and GSE28146 (independent validation) were included. Candidate MLM genes were retrieved from MSigDB. Differentially expressed MLM genes were screened by limma, followed by two-step feature selection with LASSO regression and random forest. Four machine-learning algorithms were compared. Model performance was evaluated by AUC, calibration, decision-curve analysis and subgroup analysis across AD severity. GSVA and hypergeometric test were applied for mechanistic exploration.ResultsA five-gene signature (SDR16C5, EGR1, ASAH2B, HIP1R, CKMT1B) was finally identified. Logistic regression model achieved 5-fold cross-validated AUC of 0.953 in training cohort and AUC = 0.892 (95%CI:0.768-1.000) in validation cohort. The signature maintained high diagnostic accuracy across incipient, moderate and severe AD stages. Hypergeometric test demonstrated significant MLM-set enrichment (p = 3.85 × 10-5). GSVA revealed close correlations between this signature with oxidative stress, synaptic dysfunction and apoptosis pathways.ConclusionsThis validated five-gene MLM signature exhibits favorable diagnostic performance for AD and reflects disturbed mitochondrial-lipid metabolic network. It provides a promising transcriptomic biomarker for AD diagnosis.

title: Heart failure in severe mental illness: an inequality hiding in plain sight.
journal: QJM : monthly journal of the Association of Physicians

title: Bilingua-DPP-IV: A Bimodal Fusion Convolutional Neural Network Model for Prediction of Dipeptidyl Peptidase IV Inhibitory Peptides.
abstract: Dipeptidyl peptidase IV (DPP-IV) is a key therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes, and its inhibitory peptides are a promising class of therapeutic agents. However, the discovery of these promising drugs has been restricted, as many existing computational predictors are based on datasets that have remained static for several years. Here, we first presented a newly curated and expanded benchmark dataset, then introduced Bilingua-DPP-IV, a bimodal deep learning framework that integrates features from both amino acid sequences and molecular structures. Our approach leveraged embeddings from the large-scale pretrained models ESM C and Uni-Mol2, processed through a convolutional neural network with an optimized gated fusion mechanism. On an independent test set, the Bilingua-DPP-IV ensemble model achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.764 and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.963. On an external validation set, the model also demonstrated an accuracy of 0.898, exceeding the performance of existing state-of-the-art predictors, such as StructuralDPPIV.

title: Antithetical roles of tau in hippocampal long-term synaptic depression in rats versus mice.
abstract: Synaptic dysfunction is a primary feature of tauopathies, a group of major neurodegenerative diseases that includes Alzheimer's disease. However, the normal synaptic functions of tau are poorly understood. Since rats provide advantages over mice for understanding human tau, such as expressing six tau isoforms and showing more robust signs of tau pathology, as well as offering a richer behavioural repertoire, we developed a tau knockout (Mapt KO) rat line. We primarily investigated the impact of tau elimination on long-term synaptic depression (LTD)-a form of synaptic weakening that tau mediates in mice. Low-frequency stimulation of hippocampal Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses revealed a robust enhancement of LTD in Mapt KO rats relative to WT littermates. In contrast, in interleaved experiments, Mapt KO mice exhibited reduced LTD compared to WT littermates, in line with previous reports. Together, our findings demonstrate a species-dependent role for endogenous tau in regulating hippocampal LTD, promoting it in mice yet constraining it in rats. Therefore, the functions of tau are not necessarily conserved in rodents, underscoring the importance of animal model choice.

title: Ischemic stroke: molecular mechanisms of blood-brain barrier dysfunction and opportunities for drug development.
journal: Fluids and barriers of the CNS
abstract: Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of disability and death, yet decades of therapeutic development have yielded remarkably little clinical progress. The limited progress in improving stroke outcomes is closely linked to dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which undergoes profound structural and functional disruption during ischemic injury. Barrier injury under ischemic conditions is driven, in part, by glutamate dysregulation, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress, which act in concert to destabilize endothelial integrity and exacerbate BBB permeability. Targeting these interconnected mechanisms represents a promising approach to preserve BBB function and limit secondary injury following stroke. Interventions aimed at modulating excitotoxic signaling, inflammatory cascades, and redox imbalance can protect the BBB and the larger neurovascular unit (NVU); however, aging further compromises BBB integrity and resilience, compounding these pathological processes and posing additional challenges for therapeutic development, particularly given the higher incidence of stroke in older individuals. This review highlights current understanding of BBB physiology in health and under ischemic conditions with an emphasis on how excitotoxicity, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress compromise BBB functional integrity. Additionally, we evaluate therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving or restoring BBB homeostasis. By integrating insights into BBB biology with advances in neurovascular therapeutics, this review provides a forward-thinking assessment on the future of therapeutic development for ischemic stroke.

title: Correction: Rats exposed to a low resource environment in early life display sex differences in blood pressure, autonomic activity, and brain and kidney pro-inflammatory markers during adulthood.
Temporal interference stimulation rescues dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of MPTP-induced Parkinson's disease mice via inhibition of lipid peroxidation.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra (SN). Currently, there is a lack of effective therapies to slow disease progression. Temporal interference (TI) stimulation, as a novel non‑invasive neuromodulation technique, can generate a focused electric field in deep brain regions; however, whether it can effectively act on the SN and influence PD-related pathological processes remains unclear. To investigate the neuroprotective effects of TI stimulation on dopaminergic neurons in the SN of MPTP mice and explore the potential mechanisms involved. After establishing a subacute MPTP model, TI stimulation with a 10 Hz beat frequency was applied to the SN of mice for five consecutive days. Therapeutic outcomes and molecular mechanisms were evaluated using behavioral tests, immunohistochemistry, Western blot, transcriptome sequencing, untargeted lipidomics, and primary neuronal culture experiments. TI stimulation significantly improved motor function in MPTP mice, increased the number of TH‑positive neurons in the SN, and attenuated glial activation and neuroinflammation. Integrated transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses revealed that TI intervention downregulated PLA2G3. Experimentally, TI reduced the expression of ACSL4, upregulated GPX4, decreased MDA levels, elevated reduced GSH levels, and suppressed lipid peroxidation. In vitro experiments further confirmed that TI reduced MPP⁺‑induced primary neuronal death and lipid peroxidation accumulation. TI stimulation protects nigral dopaminergic neurons by inhibiting lipid peroxidation, ameliorates motor deficits and pathological features in PD mice, and provides a novel strategy for non‑invasive neuromodulation therapy in PD. Not applicable.

title: Epinephrine-mediated sensitization of thioredoxin 1 enhances chlorpromazine protection against acute hepatotoxicity.
abstract: Acute liver injury (ALI) is characterised by rapid hepatic necrosis and compromised liver functions. Drug-induced ALI, in particular, is associated with glutathione depletion and overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These alterations highlight the contribution of the thioredoxin system (Trx/TrxR/NADPH) in preserving hepatic redox homeostasis. Previously, we demonstrated that thioredoxin-1 (Trx1) overexpression exerts protective effects against ischemic heart and peripheral vascular disease. Also, the neuroprotective role of thioredoxin reductase (TrxR1) has been reported in Parkinson's Disease. However, it remains unclear whether epinephrine (EP)-mediated boosting of the thioredoxin system, together with chlorpromazine (CPZ), provides sufficient protection against drug-induced ALI. To investigate this hypothesis, C57BL/6 mice were chronically administered a low dose of EP to enhance the expression of Trx1/TrxR1, followed by ALI induction with N-acetyl-para-aminophenol (APAP) and treatment with a subtoxic dose of CPZ. In parallel, hepatoma cell lines were treated with EP and/or CPZ to monitor the associated subcellular and molecular changes. The results showed that EP enhanced the expression of Trx1, thioredoxin-like protein 1 (TrxL1), and TrxR1 in liver and TrxR1 in hepatoma cell lines. Also, EP attenuated liver injury and enhanced the therapeutic effect of CPZ in ALI mice. A significant improvement in liver biomarkers, resolution of inflammation, attenuated oxidative stress, and restoration of hepatic histological architecture accompanied these observations. Moreover, activation of the thioredoxin system in hepatoma cells was associated with overexpression of β-arrestin1, TrxL1, and cAMP-response element-binding protein (CREB1), mirroring their involvement in Trx-mediated protection. Conclusively, these results addressed the protective role of boosting the cytosolic thioredoxin system in drug-induced ALI.
keywords: Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury

title: Developing a digital heart failure symptom management intervention using the preparation phase of the Multiphase Optimization StraTegy.
abstract: Persons with heart failure (HF) often experience bothersome symptoms in daily life, which can negatively affect their health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Self-care e.g. to monitor and manage symptoms, is essential in HF management. Self-care can stabilize the disease, reduce symptoms, and improve outcomes. However, patients often find it difficult to recognize and manage symptoms due to various factors. Consequently, many people delay acting until their symptoms become too severe to manage by themselves. This highlights the need for timely engagement in symptom monitoring and interpretation to enable early and appropriate responses. In the SympTom mAnagement and self-caRe (STAR) study, we prepare (phase 1), optimize (phase 2), and evaluate (phase 3) a digital intervention using the Multiphase Optimization StraTegy (MOST). The STAR intervention supports patients with HF in recognizing their symptoms and taking timely, appropriate actions. The aim of this study is to describe the MOST preparation phase of the STAR intervention, including its development of the underlying conceptual model, identification of candidate components and optimization criterion, and assessment of intervention feasibility to inform the subsequent optimization phase. We conducted four sequential activities from the preparation phase of MOST: (1) developing a conceptual model; (2) identifying candidate components; (3) identifying optimization criterion; and (4) conducting a feasibility study of the digital STAR intervention with patients with HF and HF nurses. The conceptual model includes four candidate components; a basic component, symptom awareness training, symptom management counselling, and symptom management experiments. We expect these components to influence behavioral outcomes such as reduced symptom burden and hospitalizations, and improved self-care and HRQOL. The set of candidate components were specified at two levels (low versus high) by varying intensity, frequency, or mode of delivery while maintaining consistent core content. Ten patients with HF and 5 HF nurses tested the STAR intervention in the feasibility study. The STAR intervention was perceived as feasible from both a patient and nurses' perspective. Patients rated the intervention as clear, user-friendly and structured. Participants valued personal support from HF nurses and perceived it as important for continued use of the intervention. The feasibility findings provide concrete input to refine the intervention prior to the optimization trial. The STAR intervention is feasible and acceptable to both patients with HF and HF nurses. Combined with the conceptual model, linking components to underlying mechanisms and outcomes, the findings provide us a solid foundation for optimizing the STAR intervention in a subsequent optimization trial.

title: Endothelial cell-specific TGM2 deficiency promotes progression of temporal lobe epilepsy by disrupting S1P metabolism and intercellular communication.
abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is a common and medically refractory neurological disorder with a complex pathogenesis. Blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction is a key pathogenic factor. As a multifunctional protein, TGM2 has been shown to participate in vascular homeostasis, metabolic pathway regulation, and immune-inflammatory responses. This study aimed to systematically investigate the expression pattern, core functions, and molecular regulatory mechanisms of TGM2 in TLE, and to clarify its clinical value. Temporal cortex tissue and plasma samples from drug-resistant TLE patients and control subjects were collected, alongside kainic acid (KA)-induced epileptic mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing was adopted to identify TGM2's cell-specific expression pattern, and qPCR, Western blot and ELISA validated its expression levels. With endothelial cell-specific TGM2 conditional knockout mice, in vivo experiments assessed seizure severity and BBB permeability through behavioral observation, intracranial local field potential (LFP) recording and Evans blue (EB) assay. In vitro siRNA-mediated TGM2 knockdown in brain microvascular endothelial cells verified endothelial functional changes. Metabolomics, RNA-seq, nucleocytoplasmic separation, immunofluorescence and molecular docking were used to clarify regulatory mechanisms, and intercellular communication networks were constructed to analyze ligand-receptor interactions. Results indicated that endothelial TGM2 was significantly downregulated in TLE patients and epileptic mice. Endothelial TGM2 deficiency aggravated recurrent seizures, increased BBB permeability, impaired endothelial function, and reduced the expression of tight junction protein CLDN5. Mechanistically, TGM2 positively regulated sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) synthesis. Reduced S1P production abolished the inhibition of RelA nuclear translocation, thereby activating downstream inflammatory genes and triggering endothelial inflammation. Molecular docking confirmed the direct binding between S1P and RelA. Furthermore, TGM2 deficiency remodels endothelial-neuron-microglia communication and disrupts neural circuit homeostasis. This study establishes a link between TGM2 and BBB function, metabolic pathways, and intercellular communication in TLE, providing an experimental basis for developing TLE therapeutic strategies targeting this pathway.

title: Polygenicity shapes distinct brain patterns and clinical profiles of bipolar disorder.
abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) manifests both genetic predispositions and brain imaging abnormalities. Genetic analyses provide a powerful approach to disentangling the associations between BD and brain imaging-derived phenotype (IDP). However, in East Asian (EAS) populations, the genetic basis of these neuroimaging changes and their clinical relevance remains underexplored due to limited integrative evidence. We investigated the genetic architecture and clinical relevance of BD and brain IDPs in East Asian populations using individual-level data from the Chinese Bipolar Disorder (CN-BD) cohort (N = 3,920), summary statistics of BD from the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (PGC) (N = 16,915) and of IDPs from the CHIMGEN Consortium (N = 7,058), and genotype and clinical data from the Chinese Longitudinal and Systematic Study of Bipolar Disorder cohort (CLASS-BD). We employed genetic correlation (GNOVA), multi-trait meta-analysis (MTAG, CPASSOC), and ancestry-specific fine-mapping (MESuSiE) to identify shared genetic loci. Functional annotation, protein association (SMR, BLISS), and spatiotemporal expression trajectory analyses were conducted. Bidirectional Mendelian Randomization (MR) assessed causal relationships, and polygenic risk score (PRS)-PheWAS explored phenome-level associations with clinical traits. Our multi-trait meta-analysis identified 11 pleiotropic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) implicated in BD-IDP pairs, showing convergent enrichment in lipid metabolism and neurotransmitter biosynthesis pathways. Fine-mapping revealed an EAS-specific causal signal (rs7941324 near RPS27P20), which demonstrated high posterior inclusion probability in EAS but not European ancestries, and colocalized with BD and specific brain alterations. MR revealed 27 IDP-to-BD and 35 BD-to-IDP causal relationships, distinguishing structural changes of the parietal and temporal gyri as markers preceding BD onset and the right precuneus area as a state marker that followed BD onset. Clinically, BD-IDP polygenic risk scores were significantly associated with depressive symptoms, anxiety, and suicide risk. Mediation analysis further indicated that depressive and anxiety symptoms statistically mediated the relationship between BD-IDP PRS and suicide risk. Moreover, PRS-PheWAS identified 135 significant associations with metabolic phenotypes, highlighting a psycho-metabolic nexus in BD. Our findings reveal associations between polygenicity and distinct BD brain patterns and clinical profiles. We identified ancestry-specific causal variants and bidirectional BD-IDP relationships. PRS associations with depressive symptoms, anxiety, suicide risk, and metabolic phenotypes highlight precision medicine potential for BD.

title: Mapping structural and functional brain networks associated with migraine.
journal: The journal of headache and pain
abstract: Although numerous neuroimaging studies have reported structural and functional abnormalities in migraine, results have remained heterogeneous. Emerging evidence suggests that neuropsychiatric symptoms may arise from dysfunction within distributed brain networks rather than isolated brain regions; however, migraine-related network abnormalities remain insufficiently explored. We integrated findings from 51 neuroimaging publications and extracted reported locations showing structural and functional abnormalities associated with migraine. Using a functional connectivity network mapping (FCNM) approach, these regions were mapped onto a normative resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging dataset (n = 872) to identify migraine-related structural and functional brain networks. Cross-sample spatial correlations were performed with genetic profiles from the Allen Human Brain Atlas and 19 neurotransmitter distribution maps. The structural network primarily involved the insula, thalamus, hippocampus, anterior cingulate cortex, parahippocampal gyrus, fusiform gyrus, and medial orbitofrontal cortex, with predominant overlap in the subcortical network (71.4%). The functional network mainly involved the occipital cortex, precentral and postcentral gyri, fusiform gyrus, lingual gyrus, cuneus, superior parietal gyrus, insula, superior temporal gyrus, and supplementary motor area, predominantly overlapping with the visual (45.3%) and somatomotor (30.0%) networks. These findings were robust across methodological parameters and test-retest analyses. Cross-sample correlations linked these networks to genes associated with synaptic function and neuroinflammation, and neurotransmitter systems including serotonin, dopamine, acetylcholine, and norepinephrine. Our findings help reconcile previous heterogeneous neuroimaging results and suggest that migraine-related brain networks extend beyond classical pain-processing regions to broader networks involved in sensory-affective integration and visual perception. Not applicable.

title: SLC20A2 Intragenic Structural Variants as a Cause of Primary Brain Calcification.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: Intragenic structural variants of SLC20A2 remain poorly characterized in primary brain calcification (PBC). The aim was to identify and characterize intragenic SLC20A2 structural variants in PBC. One familial PBC pedigree and two sporadic patients underwent whole-genome sequencing and copy-number analysis, followed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Sanger validation. Long-read sequencing (LRS) resolved complex architecture. Transcript and protein effects were assessed by reverse transcription (RT)-PCR, RT-quantitative PCR, and western blotting. We identified three intragenic SLC20A2 structural variants: exon 2-3 and exon 5 tandem duplications in F1 and F3, respectively, and a complex exon 2-3 inverted insertion in F2. F1 and F3 showed aberrant, frameshift-generating transcripts, and F3 showed reduced SLC20A2 mRNA and protein. Accordingly, the F1 and F3 variants were classified as pathogenic, whereas the F2 variant remained of uncertain significance. Our study expands the spectrum of intragenic SLC20A2 structural variation in PBC and highlights the value of copy number variation analysis and LRS in genetically unresolved individuals. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Remote Versus In-Person Follow-up Programming After Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease: A Multicenter Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: Remote programming of deep brain stimulation may improve access to specialized postoperative care for people with Parkinson's disease, but prospective randomized evidence remains limited. We aimed to determine whether remote follow-up programming after standardized inpatient initiation is noninferior to conventional in-person follow-up programming for motor outcomes during the early postoperative period. In this prospective, randomized, open-label, multicenter noninferiority trial, adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease who recently underwent bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation implantation at six German centers were randomly assigned 1:1 to conventional in-person follow-up programming or remote follow-up programming through a secure telemedicine platform during the first 90 days after surgery. All participants underwent initial in-person postoperative programming before randomization. The primary outcome was the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part III score at 90 days in the medication on and stimulation ON state. The prespecified noninferiority margin was 5 points. Fifty-two participants were randomly assigned. The per-protocol population included 26 participants in the conventional care group and 22 in the remote programming group. The between-group median difference of the primary endpoint was -2.5 points (95% confidence interval, -9.0 to 2.0), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion. Secondary clinical outcomes and patient-reported outcomes were broadly comparable between groups. Serious adverse events occurred at similar frequencies in both groups, and no deaths occurred. Remote follow-up programming after standardized inpatient initiation achieved motor outcomes noninferior to conventional in-person follow-up during the first 3 months, with no clear short-term safety signal. © 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Harmonized Protocol for Segmentation of the Hippocampal Tail on High-Resolution In Vivo MRI From the Hippocampal Subfields Group (HSG).
abstract: The hippocampus is a heterogeneous structure with cytoarchitectonically distinct subfields that exhibit heterogeneous lifespan trajectories and are differentially susceptible to diseases. Advances in high-resolution imaging have accelerated research on these structures, yet variability in segmentation protocols limits cross-study comparability. The Hippocampal Subfields Group (HSG) is an international consortium addressing this challenge by developing a reliable, accessible, and freely available segmentation protocol for high-resolution T2-weighted 3T MRI scans (http://www.hippocampalsubfields.com). Here, we present the harmonized protocol for the posterior portion of the hippocampus (the "tail"), complementing the previously established "body" protocol, and with an anterior "head" protocol under development. The tail protocol provides standardized definitions of the external boundaries for the posterior-most extent of the hippocampus, facilitating consistent segmentation from surrounding tissues. The research community was extensively involved through an online survey that incorporated comprehensive protocol details, feasibility assessments, tutorial videos, and illustrative segmentations. Through this collaborative process, consensus emerged to exclude subfield labeling in the hippocampal tail due to limited visibility of internal landmarks and substantial anatomical variability in this region. All proposed boundary guidelines were deemed clear and agreed upon via a Delphi procedure. The harmonized tail protocol has high intra- (Averaged ICC(2, 1) > 0.98; Averaged Dice Similarity Coefficient = 0.92) and inter-rater reliability (Averaged ICC(2, k) > 0.98; Averaged Dice Similarity Coefficient = 0.86) and offers a practical framework for replicable segmentation. By establishing standardized guidelines, this protocol enhances comparability of findings across developmental, aging, and clinical research and is compatible with ongoing technological advances.

title: Dimensional and categorical emotional ratings of Russian nouns: The ENRuN-2 database.
abstract: Databases with emotional ratings of words are essential for studying emotional information processing in psychology, psycholinguistics, neuroscience, and related disciplines. The emotional content of stimuli is traditionally described within two approaches: dimensional (rating words on continuous scales such as valence and arousal) and categorical (rating associations of words with discrete emotion categories). Databases with emotional ratings of words have been developed for various languages, but only a few integrate both approaches. The present study introduces the first large database with emotional ratings of Russian words, ENRuN-2, which includes 6,708 nouns rated by valence, arousal, and relatedness to five discrete emotion categories: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, and disgust. Ratings were collected from 3,902 native speakers, with data quality procedures yielding a final sample of 2,681 participants. Reliability analyses demonstrated high inter-rater consistency across parameters (mean ICCs = .84-.96) and strong intra-rater stability of ratings. High correlations with existing Russian affective norms (rs = .50-.98) demonstrate the convergent validity of the ratings. Analysis of relationships among emotional parameters revealed that they are mostly nonlinear and consistent with findings from similar databases in other languages, further supporting validity. Gender differences in ratings are negligible, and correlations between them are high; however, male and female ratings diverge substantially for some words. The ENRuN-2 database can be used in a wide array of emotion studies and is freely available on the Open Science Framework ( https://osf.io/sv9mh ).

title: Spatiotemporal Resolution for Neurodegenerative Diseases: Linking Proteinopathy, Cellular Vulnerability, and Disease Trajectories.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by selective and progressive degeneration of specific neuronal populations, often accompanied by glial dysfunction. Despite extensive investigation, proposed pathogenic models remain insufficient to fully explain selective vulnerability and stereotyped spatiotemporal patterns of neurodegeneration across diseases. Spatial omics technologies preserve anatomical context and enable interrogation of cell-type composition, molecular heterogeneity, and intercellular interactions within neural systems. In this review, we synthesize current concepts and technological advances in spatial omics and discuss how these approaches are reshaping our understanding of NDs. Spatial omics provides an integrative framework for linking pathological protein aggregation with selective cellular vulnerability, microenvironment-dependent interactions, and disease progression across molecular, cellular, and anatomical scales. We highlight emerging insights into pathology-associated gene modules, neuron-glia interactions, and mechanisms underlying regional vulnerability. Finally, we discuss multimodal data integration and future directions for translating spatially resolved molecular maps into mechanistic understanding.

title: Neuroplastin Suppresses Seizures by Downregulating Endophilin A1 to Promote Internalization of GluA1-AMPA Receptors: Therapeutic Implications of Arbutin.
abstract: Status epilepticus (SE) is a critical neurological disorder characterized by an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. α-Amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission, whereas internalization of GluA1-containing AMPARs regulates neuronal excitability. Although neuroplastin (Np) modulates neuronal excitability, its role in GluA1-AMPAR internalization in epilepsy remains unclear. Using single-cell transcriptomics, virtual knockout, in vitro and in vivo epilepsy models, patch-clamp, biochemistry, and behavioral tests, we identified Endophilin A1 (EndoA1) as a key target through which Np regulates GluA1 internalization. In epilepsy models, EndoA1 was upregulated, surface GluA1 levels increased, and receptor internalization was reduced. EndoA1 knockdown decreased the amplitude and frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs), promoted GluA1 internalization, prolonged seizure latency, and shortened seizure duration. Np overexpression reduced EndoA1 expression, facilitated GluA1 internalization, and suppressed hyperexcitability, whereas EndoA1 knockdown rescued the Np knockdown-induced phenotype. Network pharmacology and molecular docking studies identified arbutin as an EndoA1-targeting compound that reduced hyperexcitability, mEPSC amplitude, and surface GluA1 in a concentration-dependent manner. These findings establish the Np-EndoA1-GluA1 axis as a key epileptic pathway, whereby Np negatively regulates EndoA1 to promote GluA1-AMPAR internalization and suppress excitability. Arbutin, which targets EndoA1, exerts anti-epileptic effects by modulating excitatory transmission.

title: Distinct Contributions and Sensorimotor Encoding of PV and FoxP2 Neurons in the External Globus Pallidus during Perceptual Decision-making.
abstract: The external globus pallidus (GPe), the central nucleus of the basal ganglia, comprises diverse cell types, including parvalbumin (PV) and forkhead box protein P2 (FoxP2) neurons. Their roles in movement regulation and sensory processing are well established; however, their contribution to perceptual decision-making remains unclear. Using a Go/No-Go visual task in mice, we found that optogenetic activation of either population impaired performance, whereas PV inhibition, but not FoxP2 inhibition, disrupted behavioral accuracy. Electrophysiological recordings showed that PV and FoxP2 neurons differentially encoded visual stimuli, licking movements, and trial outcomes. FoxP2 inhibition produced minimal changes in the spontaneous firing of substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) neurons. PV inhibition altered spontaneous SNr firing and, together with PV activation, altered task-evoked SNr activity, reducing the preference for reward-predicting stimuli in one subpopulation and unrewarded outcomes in another. These findings reveal the distinct roles of GPe PV and FoxP2 neurons in shaping perceptual decisions and modulating basal ganglia output.

title: Association of Cholinergic Stimulation with Improved Functional Performance and Neurotrophic Markers in Mild Cognitive Impairment.
abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is frequently accompanied by early impairment in gait and postural control. Whether commonly prescribed cognitive therapies differentially influence physical function and neurotrophic signaling remains unclear. We followed 99 older adults with MCI for six months while receiving either the cholinergic agent Donepezil (n = 47, age = 68.3 ± 4.1 years) or the glutamatergic modulator Memantine (n = 52, age = 70.1 ± 3.9 years). Postural balance and gait speed were assessed using the Short Physical Performance Battery. Plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) were measured. Donepezil treatment improved postural balance (Cohen's d = 0.30) and gait speed (d = 0.45), whereas Memantine produced no meaningful changes (d < 0.20 for both outcomes). Repeated-measures ANOVA demonstrated significant Time × Treatment interactions for balance (F(1,97) = 5.9, p < 0.05) and gait speed (F(1,97) = 6.4, p < 0.05). Plasma BDNF increased by approximately 22% (d = 0.46) and GDNF by 19% (d = 0.42) following Donepezil, with no significant biomarker changes in the Memantine group. In the Donepezil group, changes in BDNF correlated with improvements in balance (r2 = 0.13, p = 0.012) and gait speed (r2 = 0.12, p = 0.018), while GDNF changes correlated with balance (r2 = 0.10, p = 0.032) and gait speed (r2 = 0.19, p = 0.002). Multivariate regression analyses demonstrated independent associations of BDNF and GDNF with balance and selected functional outcomes after adjustment for confounders. Donepezil is associated with clinically meaningful improvements in mobility in MCI, accompanied by enhanced neurotrophic support. These findings are consistent with a relationship between cholinergic stimulation, motor function, and neurotrophic pathways in MCI.

title: Ferroptosis in health and disease.
abstract: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, non-apoptotic form of regulated cell death that is driven by lipid peroxidation. In the past decade, it has emerged as a core pathogenic mechanism in a wide range of human diseases, such as neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and notably, reproductive dysfunction. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular mechanisms underlying ferroptosis with a specific focus on the System Xc⁻-GSH-GPX4 axis, iron metabolism, lipid peroxidation, and the regulatory roles of key modulators such as Nrf2, ACSL4, and CISD2. This review also explores the physiological roles of ferroptosis in development, tissue homeostasis, and immune regulation, as well as its pathological contributions to obesity, diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, neurodegeneration, stroke, cancer, infectious diseases, and reproductive disorders. A substantial part of this review discusses the role of ferroptosis in the pathogenesis of reproductive disorders, such as male reproductive pathologies, including varicocele, testicular ischemia-reperfusion, cryptorchidism, oligospermia, erectile dysfunction, and testicular cancer, and female pathologies like primary ovarian insufficiency, polycystic ovary syndrome, endometriosis, ovarian cancer, and pre-eclampsia. Moreover, the interplay between ferroptosis and immune dysfunction in reproductive tract infections was highlighted. Furthermore, we evaluated current biomarkers, emerging therapeutic strategies, and key translational challenges, highlighting the promise of ferroptosis-modulating agents for novel diagnostic and therapeutic interventions in reproductive medicine and beyond.

title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in neurology: biomarkers and clinical implications.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared downstream pathogenic mechanism across a wide spectrum of neurological disorders, ranging from primary mitochondrial diseases to conditions including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, hereditary ataxias and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies. This Review examines the role of mitochondrial biomarkers in improving diagnostic accuracy, patient stratification and monitoring of disease progression and therapeutic response. Primary mitochondrial diseases are presented as proof-of-concept models of impaired oxidative phosphorylation, providing a framework for biomarker identification and validation with translational relevance to other neurological diseases. Mitochondrial biomarkers can be broadly categorized into four domains: fluid biomarkers, reflecting metabolic alterations and stress signalling; genetic biomarkers, capturing mitochondrial DNA integrity and dynamics; multi-omics approaches, integrating transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic signatures; and imaging biomarkers, enabling in vivo assessment of structural and functional consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction. Across disorders, these biomarkers reveal shared disturbances in bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, mitochondrial genome maintenance and inflammatory signalling. However, clinical implementation remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, biological variability and reduced disease specificity. Integrated, multimodal biomarker strategies, combined with longitudinal validation, will be essential for supporting precision medicine and guiding the development of therapies to target mitochondrial pathways in neurology.

title: Disease trajectory in cerebral amyloid angiopathy: a matter of time.
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a significant contributor to cerebrovascular disease, characterized by the deposition of amyloid-beta in the walls of cerebral small arteries and capillaries. This communication presents a detailed long-term follow-up of a 75-year-old female patient diagnosed with possible CAA in 2016, who demonstrated various clinical and neuroradiological manifestations over an 11-year period. Initial assessments revealed a right prerolandic hyperdense spontaneous convexal subarachnoid hemorrhage (cSAH) and a small vessel disease pattern on MRI. Subsequent imaging highlighted the progression of leptomeningeal involvement and cortical superficial siderosis (cSS), culminating in a lobar intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in 2026. This example shows the complexity and variability of CAA progression, underscoring different phenotypes and disease trajectories associated with CAA, and advocating for a nuanced understanding of its natural history to enhance personalized management strategies.

title: Privileged representational axes in biological and artificial neural networks.
abstract: How do neurons code information? Recent work emphasizes the geometry and information content of population codes, using measures that are blind to the native tunings (or 'axes') of neural responses. But might these representational axes matter, with some privileged systematically over others? We developed methods to test for alignment of neural tuning across brains and deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). Across both vision and audition, both brains and DCNNs consistently favoured certain axes for representing the natural world. Moreover, the representational axes of DCNNs trained on natural inputs were aligned to those in perceptual cortices, such that axis-sensitive model-brain similarity metrics better differentiated competing models of biological sensory systems. We further show that coding schemes that privilege certain axes can facilitate task performance, reduce downstream wiring costs and improve generalization. These results motivate a new framework for understanding neural tuning in biological and artificial networks and its computational benefits.

title: Interneurons and network activity in the cerebral cortex: a developmental dialogue.
abstract: The mammalian cerebral cortex undergoes profound functional changes during early postnatal development. During this period, neurons generate spontaneous electrical activity long before sensory experience, coordinating into distinct patterns of synchronous activity. Traditionally, neuronal activity has been viewed as instructing interneuron development by modulating transcriptional programmes, morphology and connectivity. However, accumulating evidence in rodents reveals that this relationship is bidirectional: cortical interneurons are not merely passive recipients of activity-dependent signals but also active architects of developing network dynamics. They regulate spontaneous activity transitions from gap-junction-mediated synchronous events to large, synaptically driven bursts, and later to sparse firing characteristic of mature circuits. Critically, different interneuron subtypes mature at distinct timelines and orchestrate transitions in network activity. Activity-dependent mechanisms, in turn, regulate interneuron wiring, programmed cell death, diversification and terminal differentiation. This reciprocal dialogue between interneurons and network activity is essential for establishing functional cortical circuits.

title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

title: Registered adolescent suicide mortality in Colombia, 2015-2024: a Bayesian spatiotemporal mapping study.
abstract: To describe temporal and geographic variation in registered adolescent suicide mortality in Colombia and its ecological association with multidimensional poverty. This nationwide ecological study analyzed 4,234 presumed suicide deaths at ages 10-19 during 2015-2024 from the national forensic register (INMLCF). Bayesian Poisson models smoothed rates across neighboring departments and years. Aggregate rates combined four sex-age strata. Separate national vital-statistics (DANE) analyses compared suicide-coded deaths with two scenarios including undetermined intent. Male-to-female rate ratios (RRs) were 2.00 (95% credible interval [CrI] 1.86-2.15) at ages 15-19 and 1.05 (0.93-1.18) at ages 10-14. Total posterior rates were 4.54 (4.22-4.87) per 100,000 in 2015 and 5.23 (4.86-5.60) in 2024; no adjacent-year change had a 95% CrI excluding zero. Putumayo, Arauca and Amazonas exceeded 10 per 100,000 in 2024. Fifteen INMLCF departments had a probability > 0.95 of rates above the national comparator in all ten years. The pooled Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) RR per standard deviation was 0.84 (0.74-0.94). Including usable DANE undetermined-intent deaths increased the strict count by 22.18%; the expanded pooled MPI RR was 1.04 (0.93-1.17). Registered mortality varied by age, sex and department. MPI associations and geographic classifications depended on registration source and case definition. The findings do not establish protection from poverty and support strengthening adolescent surveillance and death classification.

title: Sustained antidepressant-like effects of psychedelics through 5-HT2AR-β-arrestin signaling.
abstract: Psychedelics produce long-lasting antidepressant effects, but their hallucinogenic properties limit clinical use. Using structure-guided design of 5-HT2AR-β-arrestin-biased agonists, we identified β-arrestin signaling as a critical driver of prolonged antidepressant-like effects in mice. Here we show that the slow-dissociation kinetics of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) enable progressive accumulation of 5-HT2AR engagement during repeated low-dose administration, approaching the receptor occupancy achieved by an acute high dose while avoiding its high peak concentration. This kinetic separation sustains β-arrestin signaling while limiting robust Gαq-mediated Ca2+ responses. Consistent with this framework, repeated low-dose LSD and repeated low-dose psilocybin pretreatment followed by a high-dose psychedelic challenge produced sustained antidepressant-like behavioral effects in mice. In parallel, these regimens produced no detectable psychedelic-associated behavioral disruption in mice and cynomolgus macaques. Together, these findings uncover the signaling basis of sustained psychedelic efficacy and provide a rational framework for developing nonhallucinogenic psychedelic therapies for psychiatric disorders.

title: Identification of candidate markers for the isolation of neuron-specific extracellular vesicles.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are present in biofluids and may be useful biomarkers to non-invasively monitor brain cells, but isolating cell type-specific EVs remains challenging. Here we introduce an approach to immuno-isolate EVs from neurons and glia based on protein surface markers. We first selected transmembrane proteins suitable as cell type-specific EV markers based on gene expression and EV proteomic data. We developed a high-purity EV isolation method and cataloged the proteins present on EVs in human cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. We then computationally identified cell type-specific candidate markers for isolating EVs from neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia. Using ultrasensitive immunoassays against several predicted neuron-specific proteins, we confirmed one marker, NRXN3, as present on EVs in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Finally, we developed efficient EV immuno-isolation methods and applied them to isolate NRXN3+ EVs. Our work provides a general methodology for the isolation of cell type-specific EVs, advancing the goal of using EVs to study brain diseases.

title: Blood pressure control before and after spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage: a stroke service audit and strategies for improvement.
abstract: In a retrospective audit of 89 adults with spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH) at a tertiary neuroscience centre, fewer than 60% met the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) blood pressure (BP) target in the year before their haemorrhage, despite most carrying a known diagnosis of hypertension. Blood pressure control and antihypertensive prescribing improved after ICH, yet most survivors remained above the European Stroke Organisation (ESO) secondary-prevention target, and the first documented community BP check occurred a median of 62 days after discharge. These findings expose primary- and secondary-prevention gaps spanning the whole care pathway and lend support to a structured, protocolised uptitration pathway after discharge, combining remote BP monitoring with pharmacist- or nurse-led dose escalation.
